groups.title: Identity
groups.prose_md:
Which company, and which earnings event. Ticker, company name, sector,
industry, country, and the date of the report itself.

Every row in the data is one company reporting once, and these columns are how
you know which one. `EARNINGS_DATE` and `TICKER` together identify a row
uniquely - if you are joining our data to your own, that pair is the key.

groups.title: Valuation
groups.prose_md:
What the market is paying for the company, relative to what the company earns,
owns or sells. Price/earnings, price/sales, price/book, enterprise value and
the analyst target price.

These are the standard yardsticks for whether a stock looks expensive, and they
matter at an earnings event because expectations are priced in before the
report lands. A company that beats modestly can still fall if it was priced for
a large beat.

One catch worth knowing: most of these divide a figure that only updates when
the company files - earnings, sales, book value - by a share price that moves
every day. So the ratio drifts even in a week when nothing about the business
changed.

`VALUATION_SPREAD` takes a different angle. Rather than comparing price to a
level, it compares two rates of change over the same year: how much the stock
moved against how much the company's earnings grew. Negative means earnings
outgrew the stock, which is the cheap direction. Positive means the price ran
ahead of the business.

`VALUATION_STATE` reads that spread against the previous quarter's, because a
single cheap reading is often noise and two in a row is not:

- `still_cheap` - cheap last quarter and cheap again
- `exiting` - was cheap, no longer is
- `newly_cheap` - cheap for the first time
- `normal` - neither quarter

Empty is not `normal`. It means there was no prior quarter to compare against -
a first listing, or a company that skipped a report - so the state could not be
determined at all. `VALUATION_SPREAD_PRIOR` carries the previous reading itself,
so you can apply your own threshold rather than ours.

groups.title: Earnings & growth
groups.prose_md:
What the company earns, what it is expected to earn, and how fast that has been
growing. Earnings per share over several horizons, sales, and the surprise
against consensus at the last report.

This is the centre of an earnings event. The market has a number in mind, the
company reports a number, and the gap between them drives much of what happens
next. The growth columns give the trend the report is landing against - a miss
after four straight beats reads differently from a miss after four misses.

Note that `EPS_Q/Q` is year-over-year despite the name, which is the vendor's
convention rather than ours.

groups.title: Profitability & dividends
groups.prose_md:
Whether the company actually makes money, and how much of each sales dollar it
keeps. Margins at the gross, operating and net level, return on equity, return
on assets, and the dividend.

Margins are the clearest read on business quality in this data. Two companies
can grow sales at the same rate while one keeps twenty cents of every dollar
and the other keeps two, and that difference tends to persist. Margin direction
also often moves the stock more than the earnings number itself, because it
speaks to whether growth is profitable.

groups.title: Balance sheet
groups.prose_md:
What the company owns and owes. Cash, debt, the ratio between them, and the
current ratio measuring whether short-term obligations are covered.

At an earnings event this is mostly about survivability and flexibility. A
company with heavy debt has less room to absorb a bad quarter, and its stock
tends to react more violently to one. A large cash position cuts the other way.

groups.title: Ownership & short interest
groups.prose_md:
Who holds the stock, and who is betting against it. Institutional and insider
ownership, recent insider transactions, short interest, and the short ratio.

Short interest is the one to watch around earnings. A heavily shorted stock
that reports well can rise far more than the news alone justifies, because
short sellers buying to close their positions add demand on top of ordinary
buying. Crowded positions amplify surprises in both directions.

Timing caveat: these come from regulatory filings on their own schedules -
institutional holdings quarterly with a lag of about 45 days, insider
transactions within days, short interest twice a month. They can be several
weeks stale relative to the earnings date, which is a property of the filings,
not of our data.

groups.title: Price & technical
groups.prose_md:
Where the stock has been trading and how it has behaved. Current price, moving
averages, distance from 52-week highs and lows, recent performance over several
windows, relative strength, beta and average volume.

Two things make this useful at an event. First, momentum going in shapes the
reaction: a stock already at a high has more expectation priced in than one
near a low. Second, average volume tells you whether you can actually trade the
name in the size you want - a thinly traded stock can move sharply on a
position that would be routine elsewhere.

groups.title: Membership & event flags
groups.prose_md:
Simple yes/no markers. Whether the company is in the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, Dow,
Russell or is US-listed, plus a few event markers.

These exist mainly for filtering. Index membership is a reasonable proxy for
size, liquidity and institutional attention, and restricting to S&P 500 members
is the most common way to cut this data down to names that trade easily.

groups.title: Risk metrics
groups.prose_md:
How violently this stock has moved, and how badly it has gone wrong before.
Volatility measured several ways, worst-case loss estimates, and risk-adjusted
return measures such as Sharpe and Sortino ratios.

We compute these from a return history ending at the earnings date, so they
describe the stock you are about to trade rather than the market in general.
The practical use is sizing: two stocks with the same expected move are not the
same trade if one routinely swings three times as hard.

`VAR_H` is the loss this stock exceeded on only a small fraction of past days,
measured from its own return history. `C_VAR` is the average loss on those
worst days, and it is the more honest figure of the two: it describes how bad
the bad days actually get rather than just where the threshold sits.

Both come in several flavours. `VAR_P` assumes a normal distribution, `FHS_VAR`
and `FHS_CVAR` use filtered historical simulation, which handles fat tails and
volatility clustering better. If you only look at one, look at `FHS_CVAR`.

Several columns in this family come as buckets from 1 to 5 or 1 to 10, ranking
each stock against its peers. Order is meaningful; arithmetic is not. A stock
in bucket 4 is riskier than one in bucket 2, but not "twice as risky".

groups.title: Event scores & season context
groups.prose_md:
Where this earnings event sits among all the others happening around it. How
crowded the reporting calendar is that week, how the event ranks against peers,
and our composite event score.

Context changes how an event trades. A report landing on a quiet day gets the
market's full attention; the same report on a day when two hundred other
companies also report competes for it. Crowding also affects how quickly the
price settles after the news.

groups.title: Post-event outcomes
groups.prose_md:
What actually happened after the event. Returns at 3, 30 and 60 days, abnormal
returns with the market's own move stripped out, and realized direction labels.

The abnormal returns are the ones that answer "did this company's news matter",
because a stock up 4% on a day the whole market rose 4% has told you nothing.
These are what you would measure a strategy against.

Two things to know. These are only populated for events already far enough in
the past for the window to have completed - a 60-day figure needs 60 days to
have passed - so they are empty for recent and upcoming events. That is a real
answer, not missing data. And because these are the outcomes our own models
train to predict, they are gold tier.

groups.title: Industry percentile ranks
groups.prose_md:
Where a company stands against its own industry, as a percentile from 0 to 100.
A reading of 87 on `ROIC_QUANT` means the company out-earned 87% of its
industry peers on return on invested capital at the moment of the snapshot.

The point of ranking within an industry is that raw numbers rarely compare
across them. A 4% net margin is weak for software and strong for a grocer, and
a volatility figure that looks alarming for a utility is unremarkable for
biotech. The percentile answers the question you usually meant to ask: is this
company good *for what it is*?

These are percentile POINTS, already on a 0-100 scale. They are not fractions
and do not need multiplying by 100 before display.

Ranks are point-in-time, computed against the peer group as it stood at the
snapshot, so a company's percentile can move because its peers moved rather
than because anything about the company changed.

On the post-earnings frame each rank also comes as a `_QUANT_CHANGE`: how many
percentile points the company gained or lost across the event. Zero is a real
and common answer - it means the company held its place - and is most common
for figures that only move when a new report lands.

A null is not always missing data. `PIT_NM` carries the reason, and the usual
one is a thin industry: a peer group too small to rank against meaningfully.
`PIT_CAPPED` flags a value that hit a clamp before ranking.

groups.title: Silver layer output
groups.prose_md:
Model output for upcoming events: our estimate of the expected move and its
direction, produced by the silver-tier models.

These are forward-looking, computed for events that have not happened yet, and
they update as new information arrives before the report.

groups.title: Gold layer output
groups.prose_md:
The model's read on an upcoming event: whether it is likely to move abnormally,
and how much bullish conviction it carries.

The abnormality model asks a single question: will this event produce an
abnormal move at all? It scores every event, so `GOLD_IS_ABNORMAL_SCORE`, its
probability and its quintile are populated throughout. It says how large a move
to expect, not which way.

`GOLD_CONVICTION` is a bullish ranking from 0 to 1, higher meaning a stronger
long setup. Each week it blends where the event ranks on the silver quality
percentile with where it ranks on the abnormality probability, among the
tradable names that week: average volume above 500,000 shares, a price between
$10 and $500, and listed options. Outside that pool it is empty - roughly a
third of scored events - because the ranking only means something among names
that can actually be traded.

`GOLD_SECTOR_ABN_RANK` comes from the abnormality model's training window and is
populated throughout, like the abnormality columns themselves.

api.overview_md:
Point-in-time earnings data for people who build their own models.

Every row is a snapshot frozen before the event and never rewritten, so you can
backtest against it without look-ahead bias. Pre-earnings fundamentals, risk and
event-window metrics; post-earnings outcomes with abnormal returns at 3, 30 and
60 days. Pull it into a DataFrame and go.

## Base URL

```
https://api.earningspy.ai/v1
```

## Authentication

You need an API key. Request one and pass it on every call, either way:

```
x-api-key: esk_live_...
Authorization: Bearer esk_live_...
```

Keep it somewhere safe: we show it once and store only a hash, so a lost key
gets replaced rather than recovered.

## Tiers

The API is layered like the pipeline behind it. Each tier reads its own layer
and everything below it.

| Tier | What you get |
|---|---|
| **bronze** | Pre-market metrics. Fundamentals, valuation, risk and event-window features as they stood before the report. The raw material for your own models. |
| **silver** | Bronze plus a quality score, trained to separate the events worth modelling from the noise. |
| **gold** | Bronze and silver plus the model's own read: the probability that an event moves abnormally, and which way. Plus the realized outcomes, precomputed. |

**What gold actually returns.** Two classifiers in sequence. The first asks
whether this event is likely to produce an abnormal move at all; the second,
conditional on that, asks the direction. Both hand back calibrated probabilities
and quintile buckets, not a buy/sell label. What you do with a 0.72 is your
business.

The boundary is enforced twice: the authorizer resolves your key's scope, and
each layer can physically read only its own storage. A bronze key cannot reach
gold data even if a routing bug lets the request through.

**Need a different column set?** If your research process expects specific
features (a ratio you trust, a filter on your universe, a formula your team
already validated) we build it as a named feature set on your key. Browse the
data catalog and tell us what you need.

## The response envelope

Every successful data response has the same shape:

```json
{
  "data": [ { "TICKER": "ACME", "EARNINGS_DATE": "2026-07-14T00:00:00" } ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJkIjoiMjAyNi0wNy0xNFQwMDowMDowMCIsInQiOiJBQ01FIn0",
  "count": 1,
  "price_as_of": "2026-07-11T12:00:00+00:00",
  "layers_included": ["bronze"],
  "window": { "start": "2026-04-01", "end": "2026-09-30", "period": "biquarter" },
  "sort": "asc"
}
```

- **`next_cursor`**: pass it back as `?cursor=` for the next page. `null` means
  you have reached the end.
- **`price_as_of`**: the freshest `PRICE_AS_OF` among the returned rows.
  **`null` is normal**, since only price-refreshed rows carry a timestamp, so
  historical rows report unknown freshness rather than a fabricated one.
- **`count`**: rows in this page, never the total.
- **`window`**: the date range actually applied, so an empty page is never
  ambiguous.
- **`sort`**: the ordering actually applied.
- **`layers_included`**: which layers contributed to these rows.

Pagination is keyset, not offset. Page 400 costs what page 1 costs, and rows are
neither skipped nor repeated when data shifts underneath you. Follow
`next_cursor` until it comes back null, and treat the value as opaque.

```python
import requests
import pandas as pd

URL = "https://api.earningspy.ai/v1/pre/bronze/calendar"
HEADERS = {"x-api-key": "esk_live_..."}

rows, cursor = [], None
while True:
    r = requests.get(
        URL,
        headers=HEADERS,
        params={"view": "calendar", "period": "quarter", "cursor": cursor},
    ).json()
    rows += r["data"]
    cursor = r["next_cursor"]
    if cursor is None:
        break

df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
```

## Feature sets

A feature set is a named column selection: the fields, their order, and any
filter, decided server-side. Ask for one by name instead of assembling a column
list.

```
GET /v1/pre/bronze/calendar?view=calendar
```

The same feature set widens as you move up a tier. `calendar` on bronze returns
the pre-event features; on silver it carries the quality score too; on gold, the
abnormality read and the conviction. Same name, more signal.
`layers_included` in the response tells you which layers contributed.

### How these change

Worth knowing if you are building against them.

**A feature set's columns are additive.** New columns get appended; existing
ones are not renamed or removed under you. If a column has to go, it ships as a
new feature set and the old one keeps working. Position is stable, so ordinal
access is safe, though selecting by name is still the better habit.

**A different universe is a different feature set, never a parameter.** `sp500`
is `calendar` with a filter, and it gets its own name rather than a `?universe=`
flag. That way what you asked for is in the request, and a cached or logged
response is never ambiguous about which population it covered.

**What you request is what you get.** Ask for `calendar` in a year and you get
the same columns in the same order, plus anything added since.

## Filtering by period

```
?period=day        today
?period=week       this week
?period=next_week  next week
?period=month      this month
?period=quarter    this quarter
```

data we hold.

**`PRICE_AS_OF` is empty on historical rows.** That is the honest answer, not a
gap. Past events are served exactly as they were recorded, so there is no live
price to timestamp.

them before you sort, or you will get lexicographic ordering and a very
confusing chart.

**`NA` is a real ticker.** Nano Labs Ltd. Your CSV parser will quietly turn it
into a null and you will lose a company. We know because we did it first.

**Post-event outcomes are empty for upcoming events.** A 60-day return needs 60
days. Nothing is missing; the future simply has not happened yet.

endpoints.description_md:
The snapshot after the announcement: what the report changed, and what the stock
did next. Built for post-earnings drift research, the anomaly where price keeps
sliding in the direction of the surprise for weeks after the news. A 30 to 60
day horizon is where the effect has historically been most measurable.

The period-over-period change columns are what most of this is for.
`EPS_CHANGE` sits beside `EPS`, `P/E_CHANGE` beside `P/E`, and so on for every
fundamental. Level tells you where a company is; change tells you what just
happened to it, and the second one is what the drift responds to.

**On the targets.** Bronze gives you the features. What it does not give you is
what happened next: the abnormal returns at 3, 30 and 60 days, and the realized
labels the drift is measured against. Those are gold tier.

picking a market model, defining the event window, and deciding how to handle
the awkward cases: a ticker that halted, a report that moved, a window that
straddles a split. It is a week of work and a source of quiet errors that do not
surface until your backtest looks suspiciously good.

Or you take them precomputed, on the same row as the features, aligned to the
same event. That is what a gold key buys you: `CAR_3`, `CAR_30`, `CAR_60`, the
expected-return baselines they are measured against, and the realized labels
`REALIZED_DIRECTION`, `REALIZED_IS_ABNORMAL` and `REALIZED_PERSISTENCE`, served
from `/v1/pre/gold/ticker/{ticker}`.

endpoints.summary: How this company's industry peers have been received
endpoints.description_md:
You have a candidate with a report coming up. This returns the companies
in its industry that have ALREADY reported, so you can see how the group
is being received before the anchor's own event.

Peers are ordered by how recently they reported, not by size. A peer
that reported three days ago carries live information about the
industry right now; a larger peer that reported ten weeks ago does not.
`MARKET_CAP` is in the response so you can see which peer is largest, it
is simply not what orders the list.

One row per company, their most recent report in the window. The window
is this quarter, falling back to the previous one per peer, so a company
that has not reported yet this quarter still contributes its last event.

**A live prediction and a resolved one never share a key.** The model
columns come in two families, and the distinction matters more than it
looks:

- `quality_prob`, `conviction`, `is_abnormal_prob` are **live**:
  predictions about an event that has not happened. Silver and gold
  tier, and what those keys are sold for.
- `pre_event_*` are the same measurements **frozen after the event
  resolved**. Bronze, because a record of the past is a fact rather
  than a forecast - and unusable for training, since the outcome sits
  in the row beside it. They exist so a caller can check what was
  predicted against what actually happened.

Which one a row carries follows from which frame it came from, not from
the caller's tier. A pre-route response holds a live prediction for the
anchor and pre-event records for the peers, because the peers have
already reported. That is the same fact stated at two different moments,
so it travels under two different names.

**The response carries the analysis, not just the rows.** Every company
arrives as a point with its raw values, its percentile rank against the
rest of the group, profitability flags, and a reason code wherever a
value is not meaningful. The distribution of each metric across the
industry travels alongside. A client positions marks and reads labels;
it does not decide what a P/E of zero means.

The metric set is fixed and `?metrics=` selects a subset of it. The
response merges two frames into one shape, so a caller-chosen feature
set would resolve against one catalogue and leave the other half
unmappable.

**On the outcome columns.** `CAR_3`, `CAR_30`, `CAR_60` and the realized
labels are gold tier and travel under `outcomes` on each point. A key
without gold receives that object empty rather than null-filled: a null
there means the event has not matured yet, and a withheld column sharing
that representation would make every blank ambiguous.

| `fwd_pe` | Fwd P/E | `FWD_P/E` | log | lower is better | n.m. when next year's EPS estimate is non-positive; no mean published; gradeable |
| `ep` | Earnings Yield (E/P) | `E/P` | linear | higher is better | gradeable |
| `eps` | EPS (TTM) | `EPS` | linear | higher is better | gradeable |
| `roic` | ROIC | `ROIC` | linear | higher is better | gradeable |
| `ebit` | EBIT | `EBIT` | log_signed | higher is better | no mean published |
| `ebitda` | EBITDA | `EBITDA` | log_signed | higher is better | no mean published |
| `fcf` | Free Cash Flow | `FCF` | log_signed | higher is better | n.m. when free cash flow is not positive (the source omits negative FCF); no mean published; gradeable |
| `fcf_yield` | FCF Yield | `FCF` / `MARKET_CAP` | linear | higher is better | n.m. when free cash flow is not positive (the source omits negative FCF); clip colour to p5-p95; gradeable; computed by the API |
| `book_yield` | Book Yield (B/P) | `BOOK/SH` / `PRICE` | linear | higher is better | clip colour to p5-p95; gradeable; computed by the API |

This is a different question from the `_CHANGE` columns. Those compare
this report to the previous one; the delta compares the SAME event
before and after the print, by differencing each frame's snapshot.

- `value_delta` - what the number did
- `percentile_delta` - what its rank against the industry did
- `state_delta` - which named state it crossed into, where the column

company's raw value can improve while its rank falls, because the rest
of the industry improved more.

applying `higher_is_better` afterwards flips the sign once rather than
twice.

`delta.points` carries the same three dimensions for every peer present
in both frames, capped at 50 - it is a second full peer read, and the
tail of a group adds little to an already dense scatter.

rolled forward to the company's next event, the response carries
`delta: null` and a `delta_unavailable` warning. A baseline is never
fabricated: a delta measured against a different event would read as an
enormous shift rather than a missing one.

a missing delta would read as "this company did not move", which is a
different and wrong answer.
